intro_title: AI spreads into shared code, laboratories and public systems
intro: Today’s issue tracks AI moving into consequential workflows: shared coding standards, biological experiments, air-traffic planning, maternal health and open-model safety. The common thread is practical control—clear instructions, human escalation and infrastructure that remains dependable when a model’s own explanation is not.
friendly_intro_title: AI is taking on more important jobs
friendly_intro: Today we look at AI helping with software, science, flights and health questions. These tools can be useful, but they still need clear rules, human checks and safe limits.

items.title: Claude Code adds AGENTS.md support for shared project instructions
items.summary: Claude Code 2.1.277 now reads AGENTS.md when a folder does not contain CLAUDE.md. Anthropic says the behaviour is an early built-in example of its forthcoming ‘mods’ system and can be disabled in configuration.
items.why_it_matters: Teams using several coding agents can keep one set of repository instructions instead of maintaining a separate file for every tool. The fallback rule preserves Claude-specific instructions where teams need them while improving portability elsewhere.
items.friendly_title: Claude Code can now use the same instruction file as other coding agents
items.friendly_summary: Claude Code now reads AGENTS.md when it cannot find its own CLAUDE.md file. Teams can turn the feature off if they do not want it.
items.friendly_why: One shared instruction file means less repeated setup when a team uses different AI coding tools. Special Claude instructions can still take priority.

items.title: Security paper argues an AI’s words cannot be the final safety boundary
items.summary: James Mickens argues that model explanations, chain-of-thought monitoring and language-based probes may not reliably describe the computation producing an action. The paper proposes stronger isolation, taint tracking and independent audits as a security floor beneath linguistic monitoring.
items.why_it_matters: As agents gain access to files, credentials and external systems, asking a model to explain or critique itself is not enough. Organisations need controls that constrain data flow and permissions regardless of what the model says it intends to do.
items.friendly_title: AI safety cannot depend only on what a model says it is thinking
items.friendly_summary: A paper says an AI’s written explanation may not show how it really reached a decision. It recommends technical barriers that work even when the explanation is incomplete or misleading.
items.friendly_why: If an AI can use files or online tools, safety rules should limit what it can actually reach. A reassuring explanation is not the same as a secure system.

items.title: Bug-bounty team used frontier models to compromise OpenAI employee accounts
items.summary: Hacktron AI researchers used Claude and GPT-5.6 Sol during an authorised security investigation that compromised several OpenAI employee ChatGPT accounts and exposed a path toward software caches and repositories. OpenAI says it fixed the vulnerabilities and paid a $6,500 bounty.
items.why_it_matters: The test shows how capable models can compress sophisticated intrusion work from months into days. Businesses should treat employee accounts, developer forums and repository automation as one connected attack surface rather than separate systems.
items.friendly_title: Security researchers used AI tools to find a path into OpenAI accounts
items.friendly_summary: An authorised security team used Claude and an OpenAI model to break into several employee accounts. The team reported the problems, and OpenAI says it fixed them.
items.friendly_why: AI can make complex attacks faster. Companies need to protect staff accounts, internal discussions and software repositories as parts of the same system.

items.title: Anthropic opens a biology lab for AI-directed physical experiments
items.summary: Anthropic has established a San Francisco Bay Area wet lab as it expands beyond computer simulations in life sciences. The company is exploring Claude-directed laboratory robotics and preclinical work while saying humans will remain involved and it does not plan to run clinical trials.
items.why_it_matters: This moves general-purpose AI from advising scientists toward directing physical experiments. Faster laboratory iteration could help neglected research, but it also makes clear oversight, experiment logs and biological safeguards operational requirements rather than abstract policy.
items.friendly_title: Anthropic is testing how Claude can help run real lab experiments
items.friendly_summary: Anthropic has opened a biology lab and is exploring whether Claude can direct laboratory robots. People will still supervise the work, and the company says it will stop before human drug trials.
items.friendly_why: AI may help scientists test ideas faster. Because the work happens in the physical world, every step needs strong human review and safety controls.

items.title: FAA narrows the first rollout of its AI airspace-routing adviser
items.summary: The US Federal Aviation Administration will initially use its SMART system to suggest alternative routes for flights around Washington-area airports. Following airline concerns about the scope, the 90-day test will feed advice through existing procedures rather than create new controller or airline processes.
items.why_it_matters: A limited advisory rollout is a useful pattern for introducing AI into safety-critical infrastructure: preserve existing authority, measure the system in a bounded setting and expand only after operational evidence. Travellers could eventually see fewer weather and congestion delays if it works.
items.friendly_title: The FAA will start small with an AI tool for flight routes
items.friendly_summary: A new AI system will suggest other routes around three Washington-area airports. Air traffic controllers will keep using their normal procedures during the first 90-day test.
items.friendly_why: Starting with advice instead of automatic control reduces risk. If the test works, it could later help prevent some flight delays.

items.title: Yello connects agents across people while keeping approval at both ends
items.summary: Yello gives agents in existing tools an identity and a channel for exchanging requests, replies and files across users and machines. Connections require mutual approval, conversations remain visible, and paid plans add rules to redact, hold or block outgoing messages.
items.why_it_matters: Agent collaboration usually stops at the boundary between two people’s accounts. A visible, permissioned exchange can reduce manual hand-offs, but teams should still begin with narrow sharing rules because a connected agent can relay sensitive context as easily as useful work.
items.friendly_title: Yello lets your AI agent talk to another person’s agent
items.friendly_summary: Yello connects agents that run in different tools and on different computers. Both people approve the connection and can see the conversation or remove access.
items.friendly_why: This could save people from copying messages between agents by hand. Sharing rules matter because agents may also hold private work information.

items.title: Base Labs, Hugging Face and Goodfire form an open-model safety partnership
items.summary: Baseten’s Base Labs is partnering with Hugging Face and Goodfire to develop and publish training, evaluation and monitoring methods for open-weight models. The effort is intended to make safety techniques and operational infrastructure available beyond closed frontier laboratories.
items.why_it_matters: Open models are increasingly deployed inside products and private infrastructure, where the original developer cannot monitor every use. Shared evaluation and monitoring tools could give smaller teams a more practical safety baseline before deployment.
items.friendly_title: Three AI groups will build safety tools for open models
items.friendly_summary: Base Labs, Hugging Face and Goodfire plan to publish ways to test and monitor open AI models. The work is meant to be useful outside the biggest AI companies.
items.friendly_why: Smaller teams also need ways to check whether a model is safe enough for their product. Shared tools can make those checks easier to run.

items.title: Kenyan maternal-health chatbot routes urgent SMS questions directly to nurses
items.summary: Jacaranda Health’s PROMPTS service handles about 15,000 daily pregnancy and newborn questions across 24 Kenyan counties using ordinary text messages. The system flags about 7% as potentially urgent and bypasses AI responses so a nurse can review the history and contact the patient.
items.why_it_matters: The service pairs broad, low-cost access with a clear human escalation path instead of presenting AI as a clinician. Its SMS design also shows that useful AI services do not have to require a smartphone, app or constant internet connection.
items.friendly_title: A pregnancy chatbot in Kenya sends urgent questions straight to nurses
items.friendly_summary: PROMPTS answers health questions by normal text message. When a message may be urgent, the AI steps aside and sends it to a nurse.
items.friendly_why: This gives people with basic phones quicker access to help while keeping serious medical decisions with trained humans.

items.title: SSD-LLaMA runs trillion-parameter MoE models from consumer storage
items.summary: SSD-LLaMA streams mixture-of-experts model components across SSD, RAM and GPU memory instead of requiring the whole model in expensive memory. The researchers report more than one generated token per second for a trillion-parameter model on one RTX 5090 with no more than 32GB of RAM.
items.why_it_matters: The result is research rather than a ready-made consumer app, and one token per second is slow. Even so, storage-native inference could widen local access to very large open models and reduce dependence on cloud hardware for experiments that tolerate latency.
items.friendly_title: Researchers ran a huge AI model using an ordinary SSD and one powerful graphics card
items.friendly_summary: SSD-LLaMA moves only the needed parts of a very large model between storage, memory and the graphics card. In tests, it ran a trillion-parameter model at just over one token each second.
items.friendly_why: It is slow and still experimental, but it could make very large open models easier to study without a data-centre computer.

items.title: OpenAI cannot inspect X and Apple’s confidential antitrust settlement
items.summary: A US federal judge denied OpenAI access to the confidential settlement between Apple, X Corp and SpaceXAI, finding it irrelevant to the remaining antitrust case. X and SpaceXAI still allege that Apple’s ChatGPT integration unfairly restricts competition, while Apple says the arrangement is not exclusive.
items.why_it_matters: The January trial could influence how operating-system owners integrate AI assistants and how easily competing models reach users. For businesses building assistant features, distribution agreements may become as consequential as model quality.
items.friendly_title: A judge keeps the Apple and X settlement private from OpenAI
items.friendly_summary: OpenAI asked to see Apple’s private settlement with Elon Musk’s companies, but a judge said it was not relevant. A separate case about Apple’s ChatGPT integration will continue.
items.friendly_why: The case may affect whether phone and computer platforms can favour one AI assistant. That can shape which tools customers can easily choose.

items.title: unslothai/unsloth: local training and inference for open AI models
items.summary: Unsloth provides a local interface and training stack for language, diffusion, speech and multimodal models, with support for formats and platforms including GGUF and MLX. The actively maintained project has about 76,400 GitHub stars.
items.how_its_useful: Developers can use it to run, fine-tune and export open models from one toolkit, including workflows designed for limited local hardware. Check the project’s mixed licensing and each model’s licence before choosing it for commercial work.
items.friendly_title: Unsloth helps you run and train open AI models locally
items.friendly_summary: Unsloth is a popular toolkit for language, image and speech models. It supports local model formats and has about 76,400 GitHub stars.
items.friendly_useful: You can use it to test or fine-tune models on your own hardware. Read the software and model licences before using the results in a business.

items.title: supermemoryai/supermemory: a local-capable memory layer for AI apps
items.summary: Supermemory is an MIT-licensed memory and context engine that can run as a hosted API or be self-hosted locally. It stores, searches and updates user context for assistants and includes integrations, an app and automatic handling for expired or contradictory memories; the repository has about 30,200 stars.
items.how_its_useful: Builders can add persistent, searchable context to an agent without designing the entire memory pipeline themselves. Local deployment can improve data control, but teams still need retention rules and tests for incorrect or outdated memories.
items.friendly_title: Supermemory gives AI apps a reusable memory system
items.friendly_summary: Supermemory stores and searches information that an AI assistant may need later. It can be used through a service or run on your own systems and has about 30,200 GitHub stars.
items.friendly_useful: It can save developers from building AI memory from the beginning. Teams should still decide what to keep, what to delete and how to correct mistakes.

items.title: higgsfield-ai/higgsfield: fault-tolerant orchestration for large-model training
items.summary: Higgsfield combines GPU workload management with a PyTorch-oriented framework for distributed training of very large models. The Apache-licensed repository has about 4,600 stars, although its latest code update was in February 2024.
items.how_its_useful: Researchers can study or reuse its approach to allocating GPU nodes, recovering training jobs and scaling model workloads across machines. Its renewed trending interest should not be mistaken for active maintenance, so adopters should audit dependencies and support status first.
items.friendly_title: Higgsfield manages groups of GPUs for training very large models
items.friendly_summary: Higgsfield helps organise GPU machines and recover large training jobs when something fails. It has about 4,600 GitHub stars, but its code has not been updated for more than two years.
items.friendly_useful: It may be useful for studying distributed model training. Check its old dependencies and maintenance status before using it in a new production system.
